title: What is the difference between IHostedService and BackgroundService?
description: Running long-lived background work in ASP.NET Core with cancellation, queues, and graceful shutdown.

data.text: **Question:** What is the difference between IHostedService and BackgroundService?

`IHostedService` gives you `StartAsync`/`StopAsync` lifecycle hooks around the host — use it when the service *is* the start/stop operation (e.g. wiring a message-bus consumer). `BackgroundService` is a convenience base class over it: `StartAsync` returns immediately after launching `ExecuteAsync` on a background thread, and the real work runs until the host's `CancellationToken` fires on shutdown. In practice you subclass `BackgroundService` for loops/workers; both are singletons with **scoped dependencies resolved per unit of work**.

**Lifecycle:**
- Host starts registered services in order, awaits each `StartAsync`
- `BackgroundService.StartAsync` starts `ExecuteAsync` and returns when the first `await` yields — so the HTTP server comes up while your worker keeps running
- On shutdown (SIGTERM / Ctrl+C), the host cancels the token, then awaits `StopAsync`/`ExecuteAsync` completion within `HostOptions.ShutdownTimeout` (default **30 s**) — after that it kills the process mid-work
- Startup ordering: `IHostedService`s start before Kestrel accepts requests in minimal hosting (they're awaited in `StartAsync` chain) — a slow `StartAsync` delays readiness; keep heavy work in `ExecuteAsync`

**Practical rules:**
- **Scoped per iteration:** a singleton service can't consume `DbContext` (scoped). Create a scope each loop pass: `using var scope = _sp.CreateScope()` and resolve services from it
- **Respect the token:** pass `stoppingToken` to `await` calls; swallow `OperationCanceledException` on shutdown; treat 'cancel received' as 'finish current unit, then exit'
- **Single instance:** by default one per process — multiple replicas of your app run N workers; coordinate work with a queue/lock if exactly-once processing matters
- **Don't block StartAsync/StopAsync** with long synchronous work — you stall host startup/shutdown
- **Error handling in ExecuteAsync:** an unhandled exception **crashes the host** (BackgroundServiceExceptionBehavior default). Wrap the loop: log, back off, continue — unless failing fast is correct
- **Producer/consumer:** pair `System.Threading.Channels` — web requests `TryWrite` (fast, in-memory), worker `await foreach` drains with backpressure; cross-process work belongs in a real queue (Service Bus, RabbitMQ, SQS)
- `IHostedService` when start/stop **is** the work: subscribe on start, unsubscribe/dispose on stop

data.title: BackgroundService with scoped DbContext and graceful stop

data.caption: Host startup launches ExecuteAsync without awaiting it; shutdown cancels the token and awaits completion within the shutdown timeout.

data.text:
Interviewers want to assess:
- Knowing the singleton-vs-scoped trap and the IServiceScopeFactory fix
- Cooperative cancellation: passing the token, catching shutdown cancellation
- Shutdown timeout awareness — in-flight work must finish in time
- Error policy: unhandled ExecuteAsync exceptions stop the worker (host)

items: Resolving a scoped DbContext directly in the worker constructor — captive dependency, ObjectDisposed/stale issues
Ignoring stoppingToken — shutdown hangs until the timeout kills the process
try/catch-less loops — one bad message crashes the whole application
Assuming one app instance = one worker when replicas multiply
Doing slow synchronous work inside StartAsync — delays server startup and health
Using a BackgroundService as a job queue when requests must survive process restarts — use a durable queue
How do you ensure background work doesn't run on every replica simultaneously?
What happens to in-flight work when the pod is terminated?
Channel vs external broker — when is in-memory enough?

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Create a scope per unit of work — the worker itself is a singleton
Pass stoppingToken everywhere; finish within ShutdownTimeout
Catch exceptions in the loop; in-memory channels for in-process hand-off
data.takeaway: Background workers are long-lived singletons that must scope their dependencies, honor cancellation, and survive their own failures.
